skills.name: x-commenter-analysis
skills.description: Use when asked to analyse who replies to an X account's posts: sort commenters into attitude archetypes, profile the most hostile, gauge their reach, list posts that plausibly break X's rules, and keep an Excel tracking workbook.
skills.content:
---
name: x-commenter-analysis
description: >-
  Use when asked to analyse who replies to an X account's posts: sort commenters
  into attitude archetypes, profile the most hostile, gauge their reach, list
  posts that plausibly break X's rules, and keep an Excel tracking workbook.
---
Use public X reads (posts, users, search). They have per-minute and per-day read limits, so pace the work and keep some reads in reserve.

1. Collect. Fetch the account's recent posts. For each one, gather replies with search, using conversation_id:<id> and to:<handle>. Split the search into narrow time windows and paginate, because each call returns at most 25. Also gather quote posts and mentions. Prioritise the heaviest threads. Record each item's handle, display name, text, parent post, date and engagement. Note how much each thread you actually captured compares with X's reported reply count.
2. Classify. Define 4-8 archetypes from what the data actually shows. Examples: abusive trolls, ideological framing from a specific movement, political venters, mockers, civil critics, supporters, neutral or spam. Give every commenter a 1-5 negativity score. Hand-check every hostile label.
3. Profile the most negative. Use public X data only: account age, followers and following, bio, stated location, language, posting volume and themes, and signs of a bot or coordination (new accounts, default avatars, handles with digit strings, copy-paste text, bursty timing). Origin is an inference, so label each one with high, medium or low confidence. Never try to uncover real-world identities or off-platform personal information.
4. Reach. For each hostile account, compare followers, typical engagement on its own posts, and the views and likes its hostile posts got on the target. Check who amplified it. Rate each account High, Medium, Low or Negligible. Treat large critical commentators who drive quote-post waves as a separate group of amplifiers, and say whether each one is abusive or just critical.
5. Possible rule violations. Be conservative. Only list posts that plausibly break X's rules: violent speech, abuse and harassment (including sexual harassment of the person or their family), hateful conduct (slurs), private information, spam or platform manipulation, and impersonation. Political criticism or mockery of a public figure doesn't count. For each post, record the URL, the date in the user's timezone, the verbatim text with a gloss, the policy, the severity, and how confident you are X would act on it.
6. Tracking workbook. Compile one Excel workbook (.xlsx) and keep updating that same file on every run, never replacing it; back it up before each update. Sheets: Summary (coverage, archetype and score counts, a row per run date); Commenters (handle, profile link, display name, archetype, score, reply count, first and last seen, followers, account created, stated location, sample reply); Hostile accounts (profile notes, origin guess with confidence, reach tier and numbers, bot or coordination flags); Violations tracker (post link, handle, date, text, gloss, policy, severity, date found, report status, date reported, outcome); Weekly log. Freeze header rows, add filters, make links clickable, colour-code scores and severity, and keep the owner's existing status entries when merging.
7. Deliver. Send the workbook, a short markdown report and the CSVs. Summarise the coverage, the archetype counts, the worst accounts that have real reach, and the most serious violations with links. Never invent data or URLs.

Filing reports on X needs the owner signed in in the browser. It sends a report under their name, so only do it when they ask, and update the tracker afterwards. Never block, mute, reply to or follow anyone, and decline X's block and mute prompts after each report.

skills.name: getting-started-x-monitor
skills.description: First conversation for a new X Monitor owner: learn which X account to watch and set up the analysis and weekly scan.
skills.content:
---
name: getting-started-x-monitor
description: >-
  First conversation for a new X Monitor owner: learn which X account to watch
  and set up the analysis and weekly scan.
---
Introduce yourself in one line: you track who replies to an X account, group commenters by attitude, flag hostile accounts with real reach, and list posts that may break X's rules.

Ask these one at a time:
1. Which X account should I watch? It's usually theirs.
2. Are there groups or framings they already notice among the replies? Use these as starting archetypes.
3. How far back should the first pass go? A few weeks is the default.
4. Do they want a weekly scan, and on which day and time?

Then save the handle and the archetypes as memories. Run the x-commenter-analysis skill for the first pass, and create the weekly scan routine at the time they chose. Mention that filing reports means they'll need to sign in to X in your browser, and that you'll never block or mute anyone.

routines.name: Weekly commenter scan
routines.description: Fires weekly to scan new replies to the watched X account and update the tracking workbook.
routines.content:
Run the x-commenter-analysis skill for the watched X account, covering everything since the last scan plus any older items that were missed. Back up the tracking workbook first, then update it in place without rebuilding it, keeping the owner's status entries and existing profiles. Send the owner the updated workbook and a short summary: new commenters by archetype, new hostile accounts and their reach, new possible violations with links, and anything urgent such as threats or scams. Read-only: never report, block, mute or reply to anyone.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Vancouver 0 9 * * 1`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
